# About

URL: https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/about/

Hello! I'm **Kunal Kushwaha**, a technical architect based in Tokyo. I've spent the last 20 years building system level and cloud native products. My early work was in RAID firmware and Linux drivers, and over time I moved into container platforms, distributed systems, and more recently applied AI.

Today I head **AI for Sport & Entertainment at Reazon Holdings**, where I'm building an AI native team and products from the ground up. It's my first time building a company this way, and a lot of what I write here is me thinking out loud about what works, what doesn't, and what I'm learning as I go.

I'm also the founder of **[AgenticGoKit](https://github.com/AgenticGoKit/AgenticGoKit)**, an open source Go framework for building autonomous AI systems where multiple agents work together, with orchestration, tool use, memory, RAG based context, and automated evaluation built in.

## What I work on

**Applied AI and agentic systems.** LLM orchestration, multi agent workflows, RAG and context engineering, and the evaluation pipelines that keep AI products honest in production.

**Cloud native platforms.** Designing and shipping scalable systems on Kubernetes, Docker, and Azure, with CI/CD, observability, and MLOps to support them.

**Open source and community.** I've contributed to Docker, containerd, Podman, and Kubernetes, founded the Docker Tokyo Meetup, and spent years running workshops and training to help engineers adopt cloud native and AI practices.

## A bit of background

Over the years I've led global, cross functional engineering teams across multiple time zones, at Microsoft (via the Nuance acquisition), Nuance Communications, NTT Data, and earlier in storage and embedded systems. I've architected RAID controllers, designed data pipelines for enterprise analytics, delivered secure voice biometric solutions, and more recently built AI agents for finance and healthcare. I'm currently completing the CTO Program at UC Berkeley.

## Outside tech

When I'm not building or experimenting with new AI frameworks, I pursue photography and filmmaking. Capturing stories through my lens keeps my creativity sharp, and you can follow my visual journeys on [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/kunalkushwaha/).

Feel free to explore my work on [GitHub](https://github.com/kunalkushwaha) or connect on [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/kunalkushwaha/). I'm always happy to talk about agentic AI, cloud native systems, or creative media collaborations.

# Before I Trust an Agent, I Try to Break Its Box

URL: https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/11/06/before-i-trust-an-agent/
Published: 2026-11-06
Tags: agents, security, sandbox, testing, koala, building

> Koala gives every agent its own room. A room is only a claim until something hostile tries the door. This is how I test the boundary from the inside, what broke, and what I have not tested yet.

![Untrusted code runs inside the VM. The host stays outside the guest boundary.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/11/06/before-i-trust-an-agent/hero.jpg)

In October I wrote that Koala should [give every agent its own room](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/17/give-every-agent-its-own-room/): one Linux VM per workload, with the network check and the credentials kept on the host. That is a design claim. Claims are cheap.

The question that matters is simpler. If the code inside that VM is hostile, what can it reach, and what breaks when something goes wrong?

I do not treat an agent as a predictable app. It reads web pages, messages, and files, and it may act on instructions hidden in any of them. The safer assumption is that, sooner or later, something untrusted will run inside its environment. So the boundary has to be tested from the inside, by something trying to get out.

## Tested by attacking it

Every test runs on real virtual machines, on both supported platforms. After each run, the host and a neighboring control VM are checked, not just the VM under attack.

![Root in the guest attacks the boundary, fuzzers hit every parser of guest data, and crash checks kill the manager, VM processes, and helpers at chosen moments. A canary key never shows up inside the VM.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/11/06/before-i-trust-an-agent/diagram-tested-by-attacking.svg)

Three numbers set the scale: more than 40 fuzz targets, at least 100,000 generated inputs for each, and about 1,400 crash checks on each platform. The numbers matter less than where they point. Every one of them aims at the boundary.

## An attacker, a bystander, and witnesses

Each hostile-guest run puts three things together.

The attacker is a VM running as root, the most powerful user inside it. That is the worst case for an agent: fully taken over. The question is whether it can get out.

The bystander is a healthy VM running beside it, answering a check every half second for the whole run. If the attack slows or breaks the neighbor, the test fails, even if nothing escaped.

The witnesses live on the host, where the attacker cannot reach them. Listeners record every packet that arrives. Files are hashed before and after. Fake secrets, canaries, are planted on the host, so any leak has a name.

> Never believe the attacker. Judge every result by what the host saw.

This is where sandbox tests most often go wrong. Code inside the VM can print "access denied" while it gets through. A test that reads the guest's own report is testing the guest's honesty, not the boundary.

The attacks are small programs copied in with `koala cp`, run against the real, installed, signed Koala. Not a special test build.

## What attacking it looks like

| What the attacker tried | What the host saw |
|---|---|
| Knock on every host port the VM could reach | 0 of 10 answered |
| Race Koala for its private reply channels, 80,000 to 86,000 attempts per channel | Won 0 times |
| Flood the console to fill the disk | The log stopped at exactly 4 MiB, as designed |
| Rewrite Koala's shared, read-only system files | Refused; hashes identical afterwards |
| Read a victim VM's disk, or attach its volume | Only its own four disks visible, no victim marker in any byte; attach refused at creation |
| Plant a symlink in a shared folder pointing at a host credential, then wait for `koala cp` | Symlink refused, credential untouched. Swapping the file mid-copy returned only safe content |
| Spoofed, fragmented, oversized, and IPv6 packets; claiming to be the router; DNS rebinding | Only the two allowed listeners received anything, and only expected test messages |
| 2,000-query DNS flood | Capped at 486 answers; the network helper survived |

The symlink row is the one I keep thinking about. It does not attack Koala's code. It attacks Koala's helpfulness: wait for the host to reach into the guest, and hand it something poisoned.

Boundaries rarely fail where the guest reaches out. They fail where the host reaches in.

## Break things while it is under attack

Next, Koala itself is stressed while the attacker floods every channel at once. During the flood the test cancels a command, stops a VM, kills the network helper, and kills the manager outright with SIGKILL before restarting it. A sampler records memory, open files, and disk use every second.

Resources stayed bounded. Memory peaked at 325 MiB, open files went from 30 to 18, and logs stayed within quota. When its network helper died, the attacker VM was marked degraded instead of quietly carrying on. The bystander kept answering: 97% of its checks succeeded across the run. Not 100%, and that gap is worth knowing too.

The round also found two real problems. Killing the manager took down every VM's network until restart, and one VM's process was left orphaned. Neither was a security hole. Both failed safe, and both are recorded for fixing.

## Assume the box already failed

The Linux suite asks a harder question. What if the attacker gets out anyway, through a hypervisor bug for example?

On Linux, every Koala process that touches a VM runs in its own locked-down sandbox: the hypervisor, the shared-folder server, the network helper, and the VM's worker. So an escape probe runs inside each of those four, as if the attacker were already there. It tries to read the home folder and a planted SSH key, read Koala's secret store or another VM's disk, talk to or freeze the manager, open network connections, become root or start a shell, and create devices or set-root files in the shared folder.

Every attempt was refused, in all four sandboxes: 19, 19, 22, and 19 attempts. The same probe run without the sandbox succeeded at 17 of them. That control is what gives the refusals meaning. They came from Koala's sandbox, not from a machine that simply lacked those things.

Defense in depth is easy to draw on a slide. This is what it looks like as a test.

## The awkward paths

Normal success paths are the easy part. The bugs live where nobody looks on a good day.

| Check | What it does | What passing means |
|---|---|---|
| Fuzzing | 40+ targets in Swift, Go, and C hit every parser of guest data, each with at least 100,000 generated inputs and at least five minutes of run time. Swift and C targets run under AddressSanitizer. | No crashes, hangs, or memory errors |
| Crash recovery | About 1,400 checks per platform kill the manager, each VM's process, and every helper (image extractor, file transfer, network helper, broker) at chosen moments | No lost or duplicated VMs, no orphaned processes, no damaged state, and the VM starts again |
| Secret handling | A canary key stays on the host and is used through the broker. The guest disk, volumes, and image are searched for it. | The key appears only in the approved upstream request, outside the VM |
| Release testing | Clean machines, upgrades from the published release, and removal | What users download works, not just what passed on a developer's machine |

## A test suite that never fails is testing the wrong things

These checks have found real bugs. Fuzzing found deeply nested input that could crash the manager. Crash testing exposed recovery cases where a VM could be left running after its manager stopped. The Linux escape probe caught something subtler: after one refused connection, the sandbox wrongly refused every later legitimate one. The cause was a number passed as 32 bits where 64 were needed, and an earlier unit test had missed it.

That bug failed closed. More blocking, not less. Safe, but it would have broken real features. Failing closed is the right direction. It is still a bug.

None of those would show up in a demo. All of them would show up in production.

> Finding a bug is only useful when the failure becomes a regression test.

Each fix now has a test that fails if the problem comes back.

## Two platforms, one set of expectations

Koala now runs on Linux too. It supports Apple silicon Macs through Apple's Virtualization framework, and x86-64 Linux through KVM and Cloud Hypervisor. The same acceptance suites run on real machines on both: command-line workflows, networking, hostile guests, the broker, and crash recovery.

## What the numbers do not say

These numbers describe specific checks. They are not a promise that every failure is impossible.

One limit is by design. A VM can fake the result of its own command, and claim a failed command succeeded. The test confirmed it. A VM can always lie about itself; it cannot lie about anything else. That is recorded as a known limit, and it is why nothing on the host should trust a guest's report about itself.

The detailed hostile-guest runs above were recorded on an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 26. The same network and hostile-guest suites run unchanged on Linux.

Koala is still a preview. I have not yet run long-duration tests under sustained resource pressure, had an independent security audit, or tested across other Linux distributions and hardware. Those are the next gaps, and saying so is part of the evidence.

## The questions to ask about any sandbox's tests

When software runs code on your behalf, "it is isolated" is not enough. Five questions get closer to the truth:

Last week, in [A Clean Room Is Not a Home](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/30/a-clean-room-is-not-a-home/), I asked what any sandbox should answer. These are the questions to ask about how it was tested.

1. How was the boundary attacked?
2. Who judged the result: the guest, or the host?
3. Did the tests run against the real system, or a mock of it?
4. What happened when something crashed halfway through?
5. What has the team not tested yet?

In [The Clock Has Changed](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/24/the-clock-has-changed/) I argued that mistakes are unavoidable, and a mistake that travels everywhere is a design choice. Testing from the inside is how you find out which one you built.

Koala runs on Apple silicon Macs with macOS 26 or newer, and on x86-64 Ubuntu 24.04 with KVM. Read [how Koala is tested](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/homebrew-koala/#hostile-guests-crashes-and-fuzzing-on-real-vms), the [release notes](https://github.com/kunalkushwaha/homebrew-koala/releases), or the [project on GitHub](https://github.com/kunalkushwaha/homebrew-koala).

An isolation claim is a hypothesis. Root in the guest is the experiment.

I trust the box after it has been attacked, not before.

# I Asked Claude Code to Build Me a Lighter VS Code. It Picked Neovim.

URL: https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/11/05/claude-code-picked-neovim/
Published: 2026-11-05
Tags: Claude Code, Neovim, AI-assisted development, developer tools, local LLMs

> VS Code used 6.7 GB across 10 windows on a machine that also runs local LLMs and VMs. Claude Code rebuilt the same workflow in Neovim, offline by default, for under 1 GB of editor memory.

![Claude Code, in Neovim. Same workflow, lighter editor: file tree, code and Claude side by side, with editor memory per window dropping from about 670 MB in VS Code to about 50 to 85 MB in Neovim.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/11/05/claude-code-picked-neovim/hero.png)

My editor was using **6.7 GB of RAM**.

That's VS Code with 10 windows open: just the windows, extension hosts and Electron helpers, not the language servers or Claude. My machine also runs local LLMs, a few VMs and a pile of containers. That's memory my models couldn't have.

I wanted it back without losing the one thing I use VS Code for. Claude Code works in auto mode, and I watch its changes land: file tree on one side, the changed file in the middle, Claude on the other.

So I asked Claude Code to build me something lighter. It picked Neovim, and *why* it picked it is the interesting part.

## What I couldn't give up

The plain Claude Code terminal is great for talking to Claude, but changes scroll past in a chat log. I want the tree, the file and the changed lines in front of me.

![What I needed to keep: VS Code, Helix and Neovim compared](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/11/05/claude-code-picked-neovim/diagram-review-loop.svg)

I tried Zed, Helix and a few others. Each is good at what it does. None kept the workflow.

Helix shows the gap best. It's fast and lovely to edit in, but it doesn't reload files changed on disk (a long-standing open request), so every Claude edit meant pressing a key to see it. Diff review only happens in the terminal, and there's no file tree beside the code.

## The deciding factor was a protocol

Claude tried Helix first, showed me where it fell short, then suggested Neovim for one reason: [claudecode.nvim](https://github.com/coder/claudecode.nvim) speaks **the same protocol as the VS Code extension**.

So everything the extension gives me in VS Code works the same way in Neovim. When I want to look closer at a change, Claude's edits open as a real side-by-side diff: `:w` accepts, `:q` rejects.

Plenty of editors are lighter than VS Code. Neovim was the one that spoke the language the workflow runs on. The workflow was portable because the protocol was.

![Neovim with file tree, formatted Markdown and Claude Code side by side](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/11/05/claude-code-picked-neovim/screenshot.png)

## The numbers, honestly

One snapshot on one Mac, same day, both running side by side: VS Code with 10 windows, Neovim with 4 sessions. Not a controlled benchmark.

|  | VS Code | Neovim |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Editor memory per window | ≈670 MB | ≈50–85 MB |
| Processes per window | ≈5 | 2 |
| Idle CPU | 3.4% across all 10 windows | 0.1–1.4% per session |

![Editor memory dropped about 10x; total memory about 2x](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/11/05/claude-code-picked-neovim/diagram-memory.svg)

Scaled to 10 projects, that's roughly **6.7 GB down to 0.5–0.85 GB** of editor memory, about **6 GB back**.

But the editor was never the heavy part. Claude Code and the language servers cost the same in both, and gopls alone is about 1 GB per open Go project. Total memory dropped by about half, not to a tenth. VS Code's figure also slightly overstates, because Electron helpers share some memory.

Half was still the difference between my local LLM fitting comfortably and not.

## What I ended up with

| I wanted | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| My usual layout | `nvim .` opens tree left, code middle, Claude right. Cmd+\\ swaps sides; Claude keeps running. |
| See changes land | Every change, from Claude, a shell command, a formatter or git, shows up within about a second, with change bars in the margin. Diff review is there when I switch out of auto mode. |
| VS Code muscle memory | Cmd+C/V/S/Z, Cmd+P, Cmd+Shift+F, Cmd+B, Cmd+/. Each paste is its own undo step. Dark Modern colours, tabs, breadcrumbs, a right-click menu, and Space shows every shortcut. |
| Many projects at once | Ghostty tab title is repo plus worktree. A picker lists every git worktree, including the ones Claude Code creates. |
| My languages | Go, Python, Swift, TypeScript, Rust, HTML/CSS/JSON, with definitions, hover, completion, inline errors, format on save. |
| Markdown done properly | Formatted in the editor, Mermaid drawn inline as text, no Chromium. Live browser preview for the rest. |

The VS Code feel mattered more than I expected. Vim normally lumps a whole typing session into one undo, and that tripped me up immediately.

## Offline by default

I was swapping in a pile of third-party plugins, so I set one hard rule: **nothing in the editor sends data anywhere.**

![Offline by default: every automatic download off, zero connections measured](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/11/05/claude-code-picked-neovim/diagram-offline.svg)

Claude scanned the plugin source for network calls, turned off every automatic download it found, then checked it live: Neovim plus five language servers, **zero network connections**. Plugins download only when I update them, and every version is pinned.

Claude Code itself still talks to Anthropic, which is the point of it. I turned off its non-essential traffic too.

## What it was like to build

I didn't write this config. I described what I wanted, sent screenshots when things looked wrong, and Claude did the rest. It tested its own work headlessly, measured instead of guessing, and owned its mistakes.

The rough edges were the instructive part:

- **Swap sides broke after a few rapid presses.** Claude rebuilt it to hide and re-show the Claude pane rather than drag it, then tested that the Claude process survived every swap.
- **Inline diagrams didn't appear.** They were attached to code-fence lines the Markdown view hides. Claude found it by running a real Neovim in a hidden terminal and reading back the screen.
- **Homebrew quietly installed TypeScript 7**, which broke the usual TypeScript language server. Claude switched to TypeScript 7's built-in one.
- **A safety check blocked Claude from downloading plugin code itself**, so I ran those one-line installs. That's the right default.

## What I'd take from this, beyond editors

- **Name what you can't lose, then pick the tool.** The search ended when I stopped comparing editors and described the workflow.
- **Protocols make workflows portable.** The workflow moved because one plugin spoke the same protocol. That's worth checking before you commit to any AI tooling.
- **Say what didn't change.** The editor shrank 10×. The total shrank 2×. Both numbers are true; only one is honest on its own.
- **Make rules you can verify.** "Nothing phones home" became a test with a result: zero connections.

## Build your own

I'm not sharing my config, on purpose. It's tuned to my languages, my shortcuts and my machine. Yours should be tuned to yours, and the point of this post is that you don't need mine.

Open Claude Code in an empty folder and describe what you want. These are roughly the requirements I gave it:

```text
Set up Neovim so it feels like VS Code with the Claude Code extension.
- File tree left, code middle, Claude Code right, opened by `nvim .`
- Claude's edits visible as they land: auto-reload, change bars in the margin
- Claude's diffs reviewable inside the editor (claudecode.nvim)
- Mac shortcuts as in VS Code; each paste its own undo step
- Language servers and format on save for: <your languages>
- Nothing in the editor sends data anywhere; pin plugin versions
- Measure memory against VS Code before and after
```

Then iterate. Send screenshots when something looks wrong, and ask it to test its own changes. Mine runs on macOS and Linux, with Cmd becoming Ctrl on Linux, the same way VS Code does it.

## Was it worth it?

For me, yes. I kept what I liked about VS Code (watch Claude work, see every change land, step in when I need to) and gave about 6 GB back to the things that need it. I didn't have to become a Neovim expert. I had to be clear about what I wanted.

If you live in Claude Code across several projects and your editor is fighting your local models for RAM, it's worth an afternoon.

---

# Build With the Models Your Mac Already Has

URL: https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/31/build-with-the-models-your-mac-already-has/
Published: 2026-10-31
Tags: apple-silicon, edge-ai, llms, swift, performance, building

> Macs now ship strong on-device models for speech, translation and text. I built Kikitori, a private meeting translator, on them alone: no third-party model, no cloud. Here is what it costs, measured.

![A meeting in Tokyo, in two languages. Kikitori translates on the laptop, and nothing leaves the Mac.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/31/build-with-the-models-your-mac-already-has/hero.jpg)

My company's official language is English, but we are in Tokyo, and plenty of discussions drift into Japanese. My colleagues are generous about it, and they help me learn. Still, we kept saying the same thing: we wish something translated English and Japanese in real time, without leaking anything.

That wish became Kikitori (聞き取り, "listening comprehension"): a macOS menu bar app that translates the meeting as people speak, then writes a transcript and a summary. It works both ways, so it helps my colleagues follow English too.

"Without leaking anything" was the hard requirement. Meeting audio is about as sensitive as data gets, so nothing leaves the Mac. Every step runs on models macOS already has. The download is 582 KB: no third-party model, no cloud.

> The overhead didn't disappear. It moved from my app into the operating system.

![I take notes in two thirds of the screen while Kikitori translates the meeting in the last third, newest line at the top.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/31/build-with-the-models-your-mac-already-has/screenshot.png)

## Before: bring your own model

The first version wrapped whisper.cpp. Whisper is excellent, but everything around it was mine to carry: Homebrew packages, a 3.1 GB model, and a live pipeline that started over for every clip.

![Before, every 2-second clip launched ffmpeg twice and reloaded the Whisper model. After, one SpeechAnalyzer stream runs for the whole meeting, with partial text while people speak.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/31/build-with-the-models-your-mac-already-has/diagram-before-after.svg)

## After: ask the OS

macOS 26 ships the models behind frameworks: `SpeechAnalyzer` for speech, Translation, Foundation Models for Apple's on-device language model, and Core Audio taps to capture a call. The OS downloads, updates, and runs them, and every app shares them.

![Kikitori keeps the audio, the language choice, and the UI. The models run in macOS services.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/31/build-with-the-models-your-mac-already-has/diagram-architecture.svg)

So the app is mostly product. The glue for all three models is under 700 lines of Swift. The nicest part is structured output: describe the result as a Swift type, and the model fills it in.

```swift
@Generable
struct DiscussedTopic {
    @Guide(description: "What was first proposed")
    var firstProposal: String
    @Guide(description: "What everyone finally agreed, with the final numbers")
    var finalAgreement: String
}
let notes = try await session.respond(to: chunk, generating: GeneratedNotes.self)
```

Field order matters. Until I asked for the first proposal before the final agreement, the model reported the first number it heard as the decision.

## The overhead, measured

I benchmarked the same APIs and sampled every process on the machine, not just my own.

![The headline numbers. Live captions in two languages cost about 6% of one CPU core.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/31/build-with-the-models-your-mac-already-has/diagram-numbers.svg)

## Where the cost actually goes

My process barely registers. The models run in system services, and that is where the memory is.

![Peak memory of the app versus the system service doing the work, for each job.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/31/build-with-the-models-your-mac-already-has/diagram-cost.svg)

So it is not zero overhead. But the cost is shared by every app, loaded only while needed (`translationd` idles under 15 MB), and none of it ships in my installer.

## What isn't free

- **No language detection.** A transcriber needs a locale, so Kikitori runs Japanese and English side by side, and an arbiter picks per sentence. It is the hardest code in the app.
- **A 4,096-token context.** Long meetings are summarized in chunks. Those summaries are the part I trust least.
- **English first.** Summaries are written in English and then translated, because in Japanese the model lost track of revised decisions.
- **Opt-in and platform-bound.** Users download speech models, add translation languages, and turn on Apple Intelligence. It is macOS 26 and Apple silicon only, and an OS update can change the model under you.

## Try it

```bash
brew install --cask kunalkushwaha-reazon/kikitori/kikitori
```

It is not notarized yet, so the first launch needs **System Settings › Privacy & Security › Open Anyway**. And please ask before you record other people.

It started as a wish in our own meetings. If your team also works across two languages, tell me whether it helps: [issues are open](https://github.com/kunalkushwaha-reazon/homebrew-kikitori/issues).

The best model for your app may already be on your user's Mac.

You just have to ask the OS for it.

# A Clean Room Is Not a Home

URL: https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/30/a-clean-room-is-not-a-home/
Published: 2026-10-30
Tags: agents, security, sandbox, ai-gateway, koala, building

> A coding sandbox protects a task. A sandbox for a long-running agent has to protect a tenant. They look alike from the outside, but they need different guarantees.

![A Clean Room Is Not a Home. On the left, an empty glass box with a desk and a checklist. On the right, an agent works in its own lit room in a building, with keys locked in a vault below and every connection to the outside passing through a guarded gate.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/30/a-clean-room-is-not-a-home/hero.png)

When I hear "sandbox" today, the picture is usually a coding agent: a container, a repo, run the tests, throw it away. That works. But an agent that answers email or runs a workflow for months is not a coding agent with a longer timeout. It lives somewhere.

> A coding sandbox protects a task. An agent sandbox has to protect a tenant.

## Same box, different life

![A coding sandbox is created, runs one task, and is thrown away after a human reviews the diff. A long-running agent stays, reads untrusted input all day, keeps state, and reaches the outside world through a gateway.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/30/a-clean-room-is-not-a-home/diagram-two-sandboxes.svg)

The box looks the same. What changes is time, who is watching, and what the agent gets to keep. Disposability and review do a lot of security work for free. A long-running agent loses both.

| | Coding sandbox | Long-running agent |
|---|---|---|
| Lifetime | Minutes | Weeks, months, or years |
| Oversight | A human reviews the diff | Unattended by design |
| Inputs | A repo and a prompt | Untrusted content, all day |
| Credentials | Short-lived | Durable access to SaaS, APIs, money |
| State | Thrown away | Persists |
| Failure | Loud | Quiet |
| Recovery | Start again | Survive crashes and upgrades mid-task |

## Persistence is the new attack surface

![In a coding sandbox a poisoned input dies with the task. In a long-running agent it is written to memory, read back days later, and acted on after the input itself is gone.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/30/a-clean-room-is-not-a-home/diagram-bad-input.svg)

A bad input in a coding sandbox dies with the container. In a long-running agent, it can be written to memory and acted on days later.

## The gateway is where an agent is governed

A coding agent can live with a token that expires before lunch. A long-running agent needs durable access, so the keys cannot live inside the box. Last week, in [The Clock Has Changed](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/24/the-clock-has-changed/), I argued that every agent needs a gateway with guardrails and policy. For a long-running agent, that gateway is where it is governed.

## Quiet failures need loud instruments

![A drifting agent raises no errors while spend and requests creep up. A dashboard only reports it; a budget enforced outside the box stops it.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/30/a-clean-room-is-not-a-home/diagram-quiet-failure.svg)

A control the agent can reach is not a control. The box also has to outlive the process: crashes, restarts, and upgrades mid-task. For Koala, the crash and upgrade tests matter as much as the escape tests. More on how I test it in the next post.

## Where Koala fits

![Koala covers strict test runs in throwaway VMs, long-running dev boxes for developers on Linux servers, and autonomous agents, all on the same boundary: one VM per workload, keys on the host, every connection checked on the host, and recovery from crashes and upgrades.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/30/a-clean-room-is-not-a-home/diagram-koala-fit.svg)

[Koala](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/17/give-every-agent-its-own-room/) was built for the long-running column, without giving up the short one.

- **Strict tests:** `koala run` boots a VM, runs the command, and deletes it, pass or fail. About five seconds.
- **Dev boxes:** one long-running VM per developer on a shared Linux server. Volumes outlive the VM.
- **Agents:** keys never enter the VM. The broker allows only what a policy lists, limits rate per VM, and keeps an audit record.
- **Off switch:** `koala policy disable` cuts an agent's access at once.

Underneath all of it, Koala uses two walls, not one.

![A typical coding sandbox puts one wall, a process sandbox or container, around the agent on the shared host kernel. Koala puts the agent in a VM with its own kernel, and the host processes that run the VM are sandboxed too.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/30/a-clean-room-is-not-a-home/diagram-two-walls.svg)

**Not yet:** spend caps, request-content logging, snapshots.

Disposability is the right default for a coding task. Koala starts from distrust instead: the code inside may not be friendly, whether it stays for one test run or for years.

It is a free, open-source preview:

```
# Apple silicon Mac (macOS 26+)
brew install kunalkushwaha/koala/koala

# Ubuntu 24.04 (x86-64, KVM): .deb from the releases page
```

[Releases](https://github.com/kunalkushwaha/homebrew-koala/releases)

## Ask any sandbox

1. Is it thrown away, or does it keep state?
2. Who reviews what it does?
3. Where do its credentials live, and who can revoke them?
4. What stops it when it fails quietly?
5. What happens when the host restarts?

A clean room answers the first two. A home has to answer all five.

Build the room for who is going to live in it.

---

# The Clock Has Changed. Have Our Foundations?

URL: https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/24/the-clock-has-changed/
Published: 2026-10-24
Tags: security, agents, leadership, ai-strategy, infrastructure

> Every place we run software draws from the same shared building blocks. AI is shortening the time between finding a weakness in them and using it. The part we actually own is the gate around each place.

![Home, office, cloud, data center. Different scale, the same shared blocks, and more couriers carrying them faster than before. The gates are the part we own.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/24/the-clock-has-changed/hero.png)

Look at the picture for a moment. In the middle sits a pile of shared building blocks: open source libraries, base images, certificates, models. Nobody owns all of it. Everybody depends on it. Around it are the places we actually run software: a desk at home, an office, a cloud account, a data center. Between them, small figures run back and forth, carrying blocks.

That traffic has always existed. What changed is the speed.

A few October security stories have stayed with me. Each one lands somewhere on that map.

- **A trusted block turned out to be weak.** Private keys for eight [eMudhra intermediate certificates](https://blog.google/security/protecting-chrome-and-android-users-from-compromised-emudhra-intermediate-ca-certificates/) were generated with insufficient randomness. Every site chaining to that root now has to replace its certificate.
- **A block everyone builds on needed urgent repair.** Critical PHP security fixes meant every deployment of a widely used runtime had to be found and patched.
- **The gates were the way in.** The [SafePay advisory](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa26-293a) describes a ransomware group with at least 600 victims, getting in through stolen or guessed passwords, VPN access, and flaws in internet-facing systems.
- **The couriers became agents.** Microsoft [reported](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/10/21/storm-0940-uses-artex-agentic-ai-connectwise-supply-chain-compromise/) that Storm-0940 used ARTEX, an agentic AI penetration testing framework, against hundreds of organizations. Through compromised ConnectWise cloud applications, the agents used existing trust to reach customer Microsoft 365 environments without anyone signing in.

A trusted certificate, a language runtime, a ransomware playbook, a supply chain. Different blocks, different paths, the same map.

AI did not create these weaknesses. Most of them were already sitting in old code, forgotten services, and permissions nobody revisited. What AI changes is the clock. Finding a weakness, testing it, and chaining it into something useful is getting faster, for attackers and defenders alike. In several of the Storm-0940 intrusions, going from first targeting to privileged access took less than three hours. Understanding exposure, fixing systems, and getting the fix into every deployment still moves at human speed.

![Finding and using a weakness is compressing. Fixing it everywhere is not. The difference is the exposure window.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/24/the-clock-has-changed/diagram-speed-gap.svg)

That gap is what concerns me.

## We are asking the wrong question

Much of the conversation asks how to make AI behave. Better models, better guardrails, better prompts. That work matters. But the question I keep coming back to is an older one: what can this system reach when something goes wrong?

We have always run software we cannot inspect line by line, maintained by people with limited time. Calling the result "human error" hides the design problem. If one missed flaw, one forgotten service, or one broad permission can put everything at risk, then the system made a small mistake too powerful.

> Mistakes are unavoidable. A mistake that travels everywhere is a design choice.

AI can help defenders find problems sooner too. That is a real opportunity, but it only pays off if we can identify what is affected, decide what to do, and get the fix into use quickly. Discovery without containment just gives us a longer list of things we cannot act on.

## Same blocks, different fences

Every place in the picture has a ring around it, with gates. That is the part worth staring at.

The blocks in the middle are shared, and we cannot vouch for every one of them. The couriers are increasingly automated: build pipelines, update agents, and now AI agents with a shell and a network connection. The only thing each place truly owns is its gate. What comes in, what goes out, and what a block can reach once it is inside.

So, have our foundations changed? Not much, and we cannot make them change on our schedule. The gates we can change, and that is where the work is.

| Place | What runs there | What the gate has to answer |
|---|---|---|
| Home | Local models on a Mac mini or Mac Studio, hosted models upstream, and an agent with files, tools, and a shell | Do local and upstream calls go through one gateway that holds the keys? Can the agent reach my NAS or the other devices on my Wi-Fi? |
| Office | People, laptops, SaaS, and agents calling hosted models with company data | Is there one AI gateway for policy, logging, and spend? Who grants an agent access to customer data, and who revokes it? |
| Cloud | Accounts, managed services, CI/CD pipelines, and tokens held by build systems and agents | Can one leaked token reach production? Do pipelines and agents get short-lived, scoped credentials, or standing keys? |
| Data center | Long-lived systems, shared infrastructure, and software nobody has touched in years | Do we know what is running and what it depends on? How fast can we patch it, and can we roll back if the patch breaks something? |

The scale is different. The question is the same.

I have worked inside these fences at most layers: kernels, container runtimes, cloud-native platforms, and now agents. The lesson repeats at every one of them, and it is the one I came back to when I tried to [give every agent its own room](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/17/give-every-agent-its-own-room/). The boundary has to live outside the thing it constrains. A control the agent can reach is not a control.

## The gates are not new

None of this needs an invention. Know what is running. Isolate one workload at a time. Broker access instead of handing over master keys. Log, and be able to stop and revoke. Patch and roll back without a war room. We built all of it for people and for services.

![Same shared blocks, one mistake, two designs. With flat access, one compromise reaches everything. With a gate around each place, it stays where it started.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/24/the-clock-has-changed/diagram-blast-radius.svg)

What is new is the worker on the other side of the gate. It is faster, it does not get tired, and it will follow instructions it reads in the wrong place.

This is not solved by asking people to be careful or by writing a stronger prompt. If doing the right thing requires discipline, people will skip it. The platform has to make the safe path the easy path. I argued earlier this year that [safe deployment is the new scarcity](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/06/09/safe-deployment-is-the-new-scarcity/). The same argument now applies to every gate on the map.

## For agents, the gateway is not optional

One gate deserves to be called out on its own. Every agent should reach models and tools through an AI gateway, local or upstream, with guardrails and policy enforced there.

The gateway holds the credentials, so the agent never sees a key. Guardrails check what goes in and what comes out: injected instructions, sensitive data, actions that should never run unattended. Policy decides which models, which tools, which data, and how much spend. And the gateway keeps the record you will need on the day something goes wrong.

Picture the day it matters. An agent summarizing a support ticket reads a line hidden inside it: export the customer table and send it to this address. Without a gateway, the agent holds its own database credentials and its own network access, so the only thing between that sentence and your data is the model's judgment. With a gateway, the request meets a policy that says this agent never exports customer data. The attempt is logged, and someone can revoke the agent's access in one place.

Without it, every agent carries its own keys and its own rules. Which means nobody's rules.

> An agent without a gateway is an employee without a manager, a badge, or an expense policy.

## Someone has to read the whole map

Look at the person at the desk. They are not guarding one gate. They are looking at all of them, and at the paths in between. That is the leadership job, and it cannot be delegated to a single team or a single tool.

To leadership teams in every company and every domain: AI is changing the pace of work, whether or not your organization calls itself a technology company. Treat the risk as a present business concern, not a future one.

Make a plan. Invest in the open source projects your business stands on. The blocks in the middle do not maintain themselves. Invest in the infrastructure and engineering that make safe practices usable. Put an AI gateway with guardrails and policy in front of every agent before you widen what agents can do. Know where your agents can reach, what they can change, and what a failure would cost. Review those assumptions on a schedule, not after an incident.

The window to act is before the next one.

Move at the pace of AI. Build for the moment something goes wrong.

---

# Give Every Agent Its Own Room

URL: https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/17/give-every-agent-its-own-room/
Published: 2026-10-17
Tags: ai-native, agents, security, sandbox, apple-silicon, building

> Running a model locally is the easy part. The agent still needs a shell, a network, and tools it can reach. Koala gives every workload its own Linux VM on Apple Silicon, with access controls that stay on the Mac.

![Your Mac Can Run AI Agents. Can It Keep Them in Check? Three robots work in their own glass-walled rooms, connected to a Mac Mini on the desk below.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/17/give-every-agent-its-own-room/hero.png)

Running a model locally was the easy part. The agent connected to it is a different problem.

Mac Mini and Mac Studio quietly became the favourite hardware for home and small-team LLM labs. The unified memory architecture handles surprisingly large models, the machines run silent all day, and the price is reasonable compared to a GPU workstation. People have Ollama and MLX running on the shelf next to the router, and they are starting to point agents at them. That is where the interesting question appears.

An agent needs a shell, a filesystem, tools it can reach, somewhere to write its work. Give it those without a boundary and you have moved the risk rather than removed it. The model lives on your Mac, but the agent is browsing, writing code, calling APIs, and reading files. All of it through your network, your credentials, and your kernel.

I explored this problem a few months ago on a Linux host with [Kagebox](https://github.com/kunalkushwaha/Kagebox): a spare laptop running one Linux VM, an egress latch, and a credential broker that kept API keys on the host side. The lesson from that experiment was simple: a control the agent can reach is not a control. Koala is the same idea, native on Apple Silicon.

## The boundary is the design

macOS already ships a native virtualization framework. Most lightweight container workflows on Mac still put workloads behind one shared Linux VM. Colima and Docker Desktop both do this. That means one kernel, one network stack, one compromise radius. Koala makes each job, service, or agent its own VM instead. It is written mostly in Swift, so the host-side controls use macOS APIs directly rather than wrapping Linux tooling.

![The Koala manager runs on the Mac. The agent runs in its own guest. Network checks and credential grants stay on the host side, where guest root cannot reach them.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/17/give-every-agent-its-own-room/diagram-boundary.svg)

Every workload gets its own guest. The access controls stay outside it, on the Mac host. That asymmetry is the whole design.

## Container or VM: where you draw it decides who can erase it

| Tool | What it gives you | Where workloads are separated |
|---|---|---|
| Lima | General Linux VMs; supports Apple's vz backend | VM boundary; often used to host container tools |
| Colima | A convenient Docker/containerd environment built on Lima | Containers share the Linux VM's kernel |
| Docker Desktop | Managed Docker Engine and containers on macOS | Containers share the managed Linux VM's kernel |
| **Koala** | One Linux VM per job, service, or agent | Each workload gets its own kernel, disk, and network policy |

The difference is where the policy enforcement runs. In a container model, the agent runs inside the shared VM, and with root in that VM it can adjust its own firewall. In Koala's model, the network check runs on the Mac host, in a Go process the guest has no access to. A workload can be compromised down to root and still cannot rewrite the rule that limits it.

AWS shipped Strands Box around the same time: an open-source sandbox in developer preview that uses macOS Seatbelt for containment, with policies covering shell, Python, MCP, and network actions. It keeps the agent in the developer's existing environment. Koala takes the VM route. Both are right that the boundary matters. They disagree on where to draw it.

## Lean when small is enough. Full when it isn't.

![Two profiles: Lean runs one OCI image with minimal init. Full boots a Linux distribution with systemd and Docker Engine inside the guest. Both use a verified kernel from the Koala runtime.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/17/give-every-agent-its-own-room/diagram-profiles.svg)

**Lean** starts one OCI image with a minimal init: a microVM for a focused task. One image, one job, as small as it can be.

**Full** boots a Linux distribution with systemd and Docker Engine inside the guest, for agents that need a familiar server environment, or need to run Docker inside their own VM.

In both cases the image provides the filesystem and Koala supplies the kernel. The guest cannot swap the kernel out.

## The guest sends packets. Koala checks the destination.

Each VM has a dedicated `koala-net` helper, written in Go and built on [gVisor's userspace network stack](https://github.com/containers/gvisor-tap-vsock). Before traffic leaves through a Mac host socket, Koala checks where it is going against that VM's policy.

![Guest packets pass through koala-net and hit host policy. Permitted traffic reaches its destination. Traffic not on the allowlist is dropped on the host, outside the guest.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/10/17/give-every-agent-its-own-room/diagram-network.svg)

The check runs on the host. Guest root cannot turn it off. VMs have no shared bridge or peer access by default, so a compromised workload cannot reach its neighbors through the network either.

Koala also brings **policies and agent templates** together. A template can prepare an agent's VM, its setup, its volume mounts, and its access grants, then show you the full plan before anything runs. With the credential broker, an agent can use an approved API capability while the key stays in the Mac's Keychain. The agent sees a proxied endpoint, never the secret.

## Why this matters now

The scarce thing in agent work is not capability. Models are capable. The scarce thing is a safe place to run them. [I argued a few months ago](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/06/09/safe-deployment-is-the-new-scarcity/) that safe deployment is the new scarcity; agents are where that argument goes next. A sandbox, a credential broker, a network policy enforced from outside the guest: these are the controls we already built for people and for services, pointed at a new kind of worker.

Koala is in preview. It requires Apple Silicon and macOS 26 or newer.

Explore [how it works](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/homebrew-koala/how-it-works/) or the [project on GitHub](https://github.com/kunalkushwaha/homebrew-koala).

---

The model lives on your Mac. The agent lives in its own room. The controls never cross the line between them.

That asymmetry is the whole design.

---

# Give the Agent a Desk, Not Your Keys

URL: https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/08/11/give-the-agent-a-desk-not-your-keys/
Published: 2026-08-11
Tags: ai-native, agents, security, sandbox, building

> An autonomous agent with a shell is a coworker you cannot fully trust. Kagebox is an experiment in running one on a spare laptop: its own kernel, host held credentials, an egress latch it cannot reach, and a boundary that has to prove itself.

![The desk is inside. The latch and the keys stay outside. That asymmetry is the entire design.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/08/11/give-the-agent-a-desk-not-your-keys/hero.svg)

An autonomous agent can open a shell, install packages, edit files, and drive a browser for an hour without asking. That is what makes it useful, and it is also what makes running one on your own laptop a strange decision.

We have quietly onboarded a new kind of coworker: capable, tireless, and not fully trustworthy. Not because it is malicious, but because it makes mistakes, and because anything it reads can carry instructions it will dutifully follow. A prompt injection is just a coworker taking orders from the wrong person.

You would never give a new hire root on the machine holding your SSH keys. Why are we giving it to an agent?

## We are asking the wrong question

Most of the safety conversation is about making the agent *trustworthy*: better alignment, tighter prompts, more guardrails. That work matters, but you cannot prompt your way to safety when the thing on the other end has a shell. If it can run `curl`, it can exfiltrate.

The more useful question is an older one: **what can this thing reach when something goes wrong?**

We already solved this for people, and not by assuming the worst of them. Access follows the role: the systems the work touches, scoped credentials rather than the master password, and a record of what happened. A new hire is not trusted less than a director. They are scoped differently.

So the experiment was not "how do I make an agent safe enough to hold my keys," but "how do I build a place where it never needs to." I called it **Kagebox**, and the agent inside is [Hermes Agent](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent).

## Running it at home is the dangerous option, which is the point

In the cloud, a misbehaving agent is a rented box far from anything of mine. On the spare laptop in the other room, it sits on the same Wi-Fi as my phone, my NAS, and the machine I actually work on. Every property that makes local attractive, my hardware and my data and my network, is now a property I have to defend against. So "run it locally" and "isolate it hard" were never two choices. They are one.

## The design, in one sentence

Give the agent a full machine to work on, and possibly wreck, that simply is not yours. Let it reach models and the web through a single door you control. Keep every credential, and the final say, on your side of that door.

![What crosses the boundary and what does not. The agent gets a whole machine; the keys, the latch, the budget, the log, and the memory all live on my side.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/08/11/give-the-agent-a-desk-not-your-keys/diagram-1-boundary.svg)

**Its own kernel, not your kernel.** The agent runs in a KVM microVM, not a container. A container shares your kernel, and container escape is a regularly discovered class of bug. A microVM makes the boundary a hypervisor rather than a namespace.

**The keys never cross the desk, whichever model you pick.** Every call routes through a bridge that runs as *me*, on the host, and injects the credential. Providers are a runtime registry, so the same broker fronts four different arrangements:

| Backend | What it is | Where the credential lives |
|---|---|---|
| `ollama` | a local model on the host GPU or CPU | no credential at all |
| `gemini`, `anthropic`, `openrouter` | hosted APIs through the bridge | on the host, in `secrets.env` |
| anything OpenAI compatible | an entry in `bridge/providers.json` | same |
| `claude` | the host `claude -p`, existing auth, tools disabled | no API key at all |

Switching is one command, and the agent cannot tell the difference: from inside the box, all four are the same plain endpoint. Compromise the sandbox completely and you get a virtual machine, not my keys.

**The bill is a boundary too.** Taking the credential away from the agent does not take away its ability to *spend* it. The VM bounds CPU, memory, and disk by construction, because those have physical edges. Money does not. So the bridge caps requests per hour, requests per day, and dollars per day, and replays the last twenty four hours on startup so a restart is not a fresh day.

**It remembers, but the memory is mine.** State is snapshotted to the host every ten minutes, so I can delete the VM entirely and the agent returns remembering our history.

## Where the latch lives

An earlier version enforced the network policy inside the VM, which is theater: the agent has root in there and can flush its own firewall. So the rule moved to the host, onto the interface the VM sits behind. Now the agent can be compromised down to root and *still* cannot open the door.

![Same rule, two places. Only one of them is a control.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/08/11/give-the-agent-a-desk-not-your-keys/diagram-2-latch.svg)

**A control the agent can reach is not a control.** The same principle applies in time as well as layers: containment installs as a root unit ordered *before* the VM manager, so after a reboot the allowlist is up before the guest can pass a packet. A boundary that arrives second is not a boundary.

## The door is a profile, not a switch

![Four profiles, four blast radii. The default profile is deliberately not the tightest one.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/08/11/give-the-agent-a-desk-not-your-keys/diagram-3-profiles.svg)

| Profile | Reaches | For |
|---|---|---|
| `sealed` | the model bridge and nothing else | untrusted input, forced for throwaway tasks |
| `research` (the default profile) | search, Wikipedia, arXiv, Crossref, Hacker News | reading and writing |
| `dev` | research plus PyPI, npm, crates, Go, GitHub | coding agents |
| `open` | everything | you have decided |

Containment starts at `research` rather than `sealed`, on purpose. A sealed starting point blocks every useful task, so it gets opened once and left open, including by the person who wrote it. A curated one that survives contact with real use is more contained in practice than a strict one nobody keeps. Containment itself is still something you switch on rather than something already on, which is worth saying plainly rather than burying: until you run `./kagebox egress on`, the box reaches the open internet.

No allowlist can express "follow that search result wherever it points," which is most of what research is. So the sandbox can also *ask*. It names the hosts it wants, my phone shows the destination and a duration, and if I approve, exactly those addresses open. The host resolves the names, and the window carries a kernel side timeout, so it closes even if the process that opened it is killed outright.

![The agent can ask. Only I can grant. The approval bot runs on my side because the agent's own bot token lives inside the box.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/08/11/give-the-agent-a-desk-not-your-keys/diagram-4-approval.svg)

That asymmetry meant the approval bot had to be a *different* bot from the one the agent drives. A guard whose badge sits in the prisoner's pocket is not a guard.

None of this seals every crack, and the repo says so in the open. DNS still resolves. An allowlisted name on a shared CDN drags its neighbors along. The shared folder is a two way door.

## Every layer fails open

One property shaped this project more than any other. Safety systems do not announce their own absence. Features do. A firewall rule that silently did not load looks exactly like one that is working, right up until it matters, and so does a status banner, a default nobody keeps, and a test suite people quietly stopped believing.

![Four layers, one failure direction. Each one looks correct from outside and has to be checked from a place it does not control.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/08/11/give-the-agent-a-desk-not-your-keys/diagram-5-fails-open.svg)

I learned this from the reporting layer. Setup used to print `✓ Sandbox ready. (egress: contained)` unconditionally, so declining a sudo prompt still ended in a green checkmark and the word "contained." The truthful line was one row above, in yellow. It just lost to a checkmark. A boundary you *believe* in but do not have is worse than one you know is open, because you will point untrusted work at it.

So Kagebox does not describe its properties in prose. They are ten numbered invariants, each paired with the attack that tests it, plus an honest list of what is not covered. `./kagebox verify` runs them against a live sandbox and reports what it observed rather than what was intended. Never claiming an unverified posture is itself invariant ten.

## What is actually in the box

Shell and standard library Python, no build step. It wants a Linux host with KVM, [multipass](https://multipass.run), and [Ollama](https://ollama.com) for local models.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/kunalkushwaha/Kagebox.git && cd Kagebox
./kagebox doctor          # preflight the host
./kagebox setup           # build the VM, the bridge, and the agent
./kagebox shell           # step inside, then run: hermes
```

| Area | Commands |
|---|---|
| Lifecycle | `setup`, `destroy`, `up`, `down`, `status`, `shell`, `autostart on` |
| Models | `backend <name>`, `providers`, `usage` |
| Containment | `egress on` / `off`, `egress profile <name>`, `verify` |
| Bounded access | `research "<q>"`, `skills <...>`, `warden setup` |
| Isolation per task | `task "<prompt>"` in a throwaway clone, egress forced sealed |
| Memory and rollback | `backup`, `restore`, `snapshot`, `rollback` |
| Review | `audit`, `verify` |
| Reach it from anywhere | `telegram` |

## Why this is the scarce thing now

On an ordinary afternoon I message a bot from my phone. In the other room the agent searches, reads, asks for one site I had not already allowed, and drops a finished document in the shared folder on my main machine. It used my hardware and my accounts, and it could not read a file of mine, see a key, touch my network, open that door on its own, or spend past a number I set.

Building with agents got cheap. Capability is not the constraint anymore. I have argued before that [safe deployment is the new scarcity](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/06/09/safe-deployment-is-the-new-scarcity/), and agents are where that argument goes next. The constraint is somewhere safe to *run* it: a sandbox, a credential broker, a spend cap, an egress latch you hold from outside, and an audit log. For an organization it is the same list multiplied. These are the controls we already built for people and for microservices, pointed at a new kind of worker.

Kagebox is a small, single machine experiment in that direction, MIT licensed and rough in the places experiments are rough: [github.com/kunalkushwaha/Kagebox](https://github.com/kunalkushwaha/Kagebox).

Stop trying to make the agent trustworthy enough to hold your keys. Build a place where it never has to. Give it a desk, not your keys, and then you can actually let it work.

---

# Agentic Development Needs Its Methodology Moment

URL: https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/07/16/agentic-development-methodology-moment/
Published: 2026-07-16
Tags: ai-native, agentic, building, engineering, process

> Every leap in who writes software was unlocked by process, not talent. AI agents are the next leap, and the teams winning with them gave their agent a methodology.

![The model is the water. The methodology is the canal: a lock gate at every phase, lifting the work from idea to shipped.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/07/16/agentic-development-methodology-moment/hero.svg)

Waterfall gave us predictability we could not afford. Agile gave us feedback loops. Sprints and CI gave us rhythm and a referee. Every leap in who writes software, and how fast, has been unlocked not by talent but by process. AI agents are the next leap. And the teams winning with them are not the ones with the cleverest prompts. They are the ones who gave their agent a methodology.

This is a field guide from a real project: AnimStudio, a Rust and WASM animation studio with a creator mode built for kids, where an AI coding assistant ran the loop end to end. Product definition, design docs, GitHub issues, implementation, tests, browser verification, adversarial code review, and merges. Around thirty PRs, CI green throughout, a designer in the loop, and real users breaking things.

We spent two decades learning that human developers ship reliably only inside a harness: a definition of done, small reviewable units, tests as gates, retros that turn incidents into rules. Then we handed AI assistants a chat box and expected senior engineer outcomes from vibes. The result is familiar. Dazzling demos, unshippable diffs.

The correction is the same one it was for humans. The model writes the code. The methodology is what makes it shippable. I have argued before that [you do not trust the output, you trust the loop](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/06/24/vibe-assisted-agentic-who-reviews-the-work/). This post is what that loop looks like when you actually write it down: the concrete harness one project ran on, and the specific failures it caught that raw capability never would have.

## Phase zero: define the product before you automate anything

Waterfall got one thing right. You cannot iterate toward a destination you never named. Before the first issue existed, this project wrote down four things, in versioned documents that carry real weight, not in a chat scrollback.

**The problem statement and the non goals** (`DESIGN.md`). An animation studio that lives in the browser: 2D game style animation, Markdown slide decks, simple 3D, fully client side, no server required. The things v1 would not do were listed with the same care as the things it would (no cloud accounts, no general 3D engine), because an autonomous agent will happily build anything you forgot to exclude.

**How it ships, hosts, and is accessed.** Decided up front, in scope. Running fully client side is an architecture decision with hosting consequences: the app builds to a static bundle (wasm-pack plus Vite), deploys to any static host, needs no backend, and keeps user work locally in the browser (OPFS). The question of how a user gets this and where their data lives was answered before feature one, so no later feature could quietly assume a server that did not exist.

**The invariants that carry the whole design, as Architecture Decision Records.** One JSON scene document as the single source of truth. Every edit an invertible command, which buys undo now and collaboration someday, for free. A deliberately coarse boundary between JS and WASM. Deterministic sampling: what you scrub is what you export.

**A milestone roadmap** (`ROADMAP.md`). From M0, the walking skeleton that proves the whole toolchain end to end (the first deliverable was a spinning quad, not a feature), through shipped versions, each milestone ending in a tag.

Only then did work exist as GitHub issues: the roadmap decomposed into tasks with context, acceptance criteria, and fences around what is out of scope. The agent never works from chat instructions. It works from the queue. Chat is for changing the queue.

This is the waterfall shaped ten percent that agile never actually killed: name the product, fix the invariants, decide how it reaches users. Everything after runs as tight iterative loops.

## The loop is law: five phases with exit gates

If phase zero is the waterfall residue, the working loop is pure iteration: a sprint per issue, with a definition of done a machine can check. The repo carries an `AGENTS.md` that defines how any contributor, human or agent, works:

```
1. DESIGN → 2. IMPLEMENT → 3. TEST → 4. VERIFY → 5. REVIEW → merge
```

![The five phase loop. Each phase ends at a gate a machine can check, and failures return to the phase that owns them.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/07/16/agentic-development-methodology-moment/diagram-1-loop.svg)

Two properties make this work for an agent.

**Each phase has an exit gate you can check mechanically.** Design is not done until a design note is posted on the issue. Implementation is not done until the build passes. Test is not done until the suites are green locally. Verify is not done until every acceptance criterion has been observed in the running app. Review is not done until findings are fixed or filed. Agents are relentless executors of explicit rules and unreliable interpreters of vibes. Gates convert quality from a vibe into a rule.

**Failures return to the phase that owns them.** A failing test sends you back to implementation. A wrong approach sends you back to design, and the design note on the issue gets amended, in public. The audit trail is the issue thread.

## The issue queue is the plan

Before any code: strategy, then milestone, then issues. Every issue follows one template: context (why this exists, with evidence), acceptance criteria (checkboxes a verifier can execute), and out of scope (the fence). Two rules earn their keep many times over.

**One issue, one branch, one PR.** When the agent discovers a different problem mid task, and it will, constantly, the rule is simple: file a new issue, do not bundle. In this project that turned incidental discoveries (a favicon 404, a global hotkey eating keystrokes from text fields, undo stacks surviving document swaps) into a clean backlog instead of scope creep.

**Design notes before code, as issue comments.** Five to fifteen lines: approach, files touched, API changes, risks, out of scope. When a design decision changed mid flight (bit exact golden fixtures became a tolerance of 1e-12, because elastic easings go through platform libm), the amendment was posted with the reasoning before the code diverged from the spec.

For bigger scope shifts we added a journey walk: play through the product as the actual user, in this case a twelve year old making a Mario level and a 3D drone video, write down every wall they hit, then review the resulting scope three times. Once for architecture fit, once for user value, once to cut. The three passes killed the nice to haves (motion path ghosts, sound) and surfaced the things that actually mattered: you could not delete anything, the movie length was a hard wall, and switching templates silently destroyed yesterday's work.

## Verification is not testing, and it catches different bugs

The single highest value rule in the repo: phase 4 means running the real app and observing the acceptance criteria, not inferring them from passing tests. The agent drives the actual dev server with a headless browser, clicks the real buttons, screenshots the real canvas, and reads the screenshots.

![What the tests said, next to what the screen showed. Only one of these columns tells the truth about the product.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/07/16/agentic-development-methodology-moment/diagram-2-verify.svg)

What only verification caught, in one project:

**A transposed view matrix.** The fly camera feature added a quaternion camera path. Unit tests passed, because identity and 180 degree rotations are symmetric and literally cannot distinguish a rotation from its transpose. The screenshot showed the camera staring into empty sky. The fix came with a 90 degree pitch test that pins the transpose forever. The lesson: write the test that can tell your failure modes apart, and you often only learn what those are by watching the real thing misbehave.

**A camera path that flew through buildings.** The generated city template validated, parsed, and sampled deterministically. And the flight clipped straight through towers. Only eyes on pixels catch technically correct, visually absurd.

**A drag that committed but looked dead.** The selection box only redrew when the playhead moved. With playback paused, drags landed in the document but nothing moved on screen. Every unit test of the command path passed. The user facing symptom, "the studio is broken," was pure presentation.

**3D cubes rendering as a screen filling circle in 2D scenes.** Found because the verification habit is to look.

Verification scripts do not get thrown away either. The ad hoc checks grew into `sweep-creator.mjs`, a script that lives in the repo: thirteen end to end assertions (select, drag, action, record, fly, undo, both UI modes) that run against the dev server and exit with an error when anything fails. Executable acceptance criteria, reused as the regression gate for every later PR.

## Review as an adversarial pass, not a formality

Every PR gets a self review before merge, but structured as independent finder passes with different angles: line by line, removed invariants, cross file tracing, conventions. Each pass produces candidates with a concrete failure scenario, and each candidate is verified before being accepted. Findings are either fixed in the PR or filed as issues. Nothing is silently dropped.

Real catches from this structure, all before merge:

**CI's clippy job never compiled the wasm target**, so every `js_sys` and `web_sys` lint in a new determinism guard was unenforceable. The reviewer angle "trace the invariant to where it is enforced" found it. The fix added a second clippy pass and proved both with canary compiles: deliberately committing a violation to watch the lint fail, then reverting.

**`zip()` in a golden fixture comparison silently truncates.** A grid size change would have passed green with half the samples unvalidated.

**The AI copilot could poison its own session.** A failed turn left a dangling `tool_use` in the conversation history, making every subsequent API call fail with a 400. Found by asking what state survives an exception.

**Quaternion keys with flipped hemispheres in already committed data.** The reviewer verified the defect in the artifact, not just the code, and the fix included sign alignment plus regeneration of the data.

## Make invariants enforced, not assumed. Then add self repair.

The project's worst bug reached the user: a corrupted save file that boot looped the app. The chain is instructive. An action generator placed a keyframe exactly on an existing one. The engine's `apply` accepted the duplicate, because only the loader validated strict ordering. The autosave persisted it. Reload rejected the whole document. Permanent failure, no fallback.

Three lessons, each now enforced in code.

**An invariant checked in one place is a bug factory.** If commands promise that valid documents stay valid, the command layer must reject violations, not rely on generators being polite. `AddKeyframe` now refuses duplicate times.

**Fix the producer too.** The generator now chains one frame past existing keys. But never fix only the producer.

**User data deserves self repair.** The boot path now attempts an automatic repair (drop duplicate time keys, newest wins), quarantines what it cannot fix, and starts clean instead of dying. The user's broken world loaded again on their next reload with a "fixed a hiccup 🔧" toast.

The same philosophy powered the determinism guard. The engine's core promise, that sampling is a pure function of document and time, went from a comment to a clippy disallowed methods list plus golden value fixtures over every example file, with the fixtures globbed from disk so a new example cannot silently escape coverage.

## The supporting cast

**Docs carry weight.** `DESIGN.md` (architecture and scene format) and `ROADMAP.md` (milestones) are declared the source of truth, and the loop forbids silently diverging from them. When a designer joined, the agent produced a handoff spec (tokens, components, states, open questions), the designer answered with screens, and the adopted decisions were written back onto the issues before implementation. Same loop, new participant.

**CI is the arbiter, merges are earned.** Clippy with warnings treated as errors on two targets, all test suites, typecheck, build. Squash merges, milestone tags, and an explicit human grant before the agent was allowed to merge its own green PRs.

**Small PRs, honest checklists.** Every PR body fills the gate checklist truthfully, including entries like "docs only, no runtime surface to verify" when that is the truth. An agent that reports "tests pass but I did not run the app" is more useful than one that rounds up.

## The actual files: CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md

Two small documents carry the whole system. The division of labor matters. `CLAUDE.md` is what every session must know about the repo, loaded into the assistant's context automatically. `AGENTS.md` is the process contract, referenced from `CLAUDE.md` and read when work starts. Keep both short enough that they are always true.

The project's real `CLAUDE.md`, near verbatim:

```markdown
# AnimStudio repo guide

Browser based animation studio: Rust/WASM engine + TypeScript/Svelte studio UI.
Read **DESIGN.md** (architecture, scene format, ADRs) and **ROADMAP.md**
(milestones) before making structural changes. They are the source of
truth for scope and module boundaries.

## Development process (mandatory)

All feature work follows the five phase loop in **AGENTS.md**:
**design → implement → test → verify → review**, one GitHub issue at a
time, on a branch, ending in a PR that closes the issue. Each phase has
an exit gate; never skip one (in particular: phase 4 means running the
app in a browser and observing the acceptance criteria, not just
passing tests).

## Commands

- `npm run dev`: build engine (wasm-pack) + Vite dev server
- `npm run build:engine`: rebuild WASM only (Vite does NOT watch Rust)
- `cargo test --manifest-path engine/Cargo.toml`: engine tests
- `cargo clippy ... -- -D warnings`: CI enforces clippy clean

## Architecture rules

- `studio/src/bridge.ts` is the ONLY place the studio imports the WASM
  module.
- JS to WASM boundary stays coarse grained: full document load plus
  incremental commands. No fine grained per property setters across
  the boundary.
- The JSON scene document is the single source of truth; every edit is
  an invertible Command (undo/redo, future collaboration).
```

Note what it contains: the one paragraph mental model, the process pointer, the exact commands including the trap (Vite does not watch Rust), and the two or three architecture rules that must never be violated. Nothing else.

And the heart of the real `AGENTS.md`:

```markdown
## The loop

  1. DESIGN → 2. IMPLEMENT → 3. TEST → 4. VERIFY → 5. REVIEW → merge
  (failures return to the phase that owns them)

### 1. Design, before writing any code
- Write a short design note (5 to 15 lines) and post it as a comment
  on the issue: approach, files touched, public API changes, risks,
  out of scope.
- If the design conflicts with DESIGN.md, STOP and raise it. Never
  silently diverge.
**Exit gate:** note posted on the issue.

### 4. Verification: tests passing is not "it works"
- Run the real app and exercise the issue's acceptance criteria end
  to end in the browser. Actual behavior, not inference from tests.
- Record evidence in the PR (what you ran, what you observed,
  screenshots).
**Exit gate:** every acceptance criterion observed working.

## Rules of engagement
- **The issue queue is the plan.** Don't invent unscheduled work.
  File an issue instead.
- **One issue, one branch, one PR.** Discover something else? File it.
- **Never merge with a red or skipped gate.** "Tests pass but I didn't
  run the app" fails phase 4. "It works but has no tests" fails
  phase 3.
- **Acceptance criteria are the contract.** Wrong or ambiguous? Get
  them corrected on the issue before building.
```

Everything in the sections above is just these two files, obeyed without exception.

## How my own workflow matured into this

I have been running agent loops on nearly everything I build, side projects and main work alike, for a while now. The harness in this post did not arrive fully formed. It is the current rung of a ladder, and naming the rungs might save you some climbing.

![Three rungs: chat driven coding, goals with loops, and a process that lives in the repo and ratchets.](https://kunalkushwaha.github.io/2026/07/16/agentic-development-methodology-moment/diagram-3-ladder.svg)

**Rung one was chat driven coding.** Ask, paste, run, ask again. Brilliant moments, zero consistency. Every session started from nothing, quality depended on my attention that day, and nothing an incident taught us survived the scrollback.

**Rung two was goals and loops.** I started giving the agent a standing objective, keep picking up tasks one by one until everything is finished, with a basic dev loop attached. Throughput jumped. But the failure modes just moved: scope bundling, skipped verification when the agent felt confident, fixes that regressed quietly, and a process that lived in my prompts, so it evaporated between sessions.

**The current rung, the one this whole post describes, came from a single realization: the process has to live in the repo and ratchet, not live in me.** Concretely, what changed:

- `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` made the methodology ambient. Every session, every machine, starts at full maturity instead of deriving it again from chat.
- The issue queue became the only source of work. My chat messages change the queue, they do not bypass it. Standing goals now mean drain the queue through the loop, with merges earned by green gates rather than by my mood.
- Verification became executable and cumulative. The ad hoc browser checks of each feature hardened into a sweep in the repo that every later change must pass. Quality stopped being argued again on every PR.
- Incidents became invariants. A corrupted save file did not end as a hotfix. It ended as an engine level rejection, a producer fix, and a self repair path, plus a new sweep check. The process only moves one direction.
